newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Lyonnais shares jump on profit hope.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lyonnais shares jump on profit hope.

text.p: Investors piled into shares of state-controlled Credit Lyonnais on Thursday, driving them up 6.3 percent, after a newspaper report that the long troubled bank expected to produce A spectacular profit recovery in 1997.

The share action came on a day when the European Commission threatened tough conditions for approving new state aid ahead of privatisation for the bank whose 1980's expansion binge turned made it briefly the world's largest bank outside Japan.

"Assets will have to be sold," an EU spokesman said on the eve of Friday's expected French government submission to the commission of a new rescue plan for the bank that lost 21 billion francs ($3.7 billion) between 1992-94 after its wild lending binge.

The newspaper Les Echos said the bank, which lost 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994 from a wild lending spree, could report a net attributable profit of 3.4 to 3.7 billion francs in 1997 after a profit of close to 300 million francs for 1996.
Credit Lyonnais would not comment on the figures the paper said were presented at a December board meeting. But an official familiar with its outlook said they did not seem out of line.
The non-voting shares, which are known formally as investment certificates and make up 20 percent of the bank's capital, closed up 11.80 francs at 198.40 francs.

Some analysts said the stock could go much higher but a lot would hinge on the government's multi-billion franc restructuring plan to ready the bank for privatisation, due to be presented to the European Commission for approval by Friday.
They cautioned the shares were a still a speculative play.
One brokerage, Dupont-Denant which raised its rating on the bank to market performer from underperformer, estimated the government would need to inject 15 billion francs into the bank.

That would involve nine billion francs to offset capital losses on asset sales ordered by the Commission and six billion francs to raise the bank's Tier One solvability ratio to six percent from 4.5 percent, seen as necessary to attract buyers.
Analysts believe the new capital injection -- the fourth in as many years for Credit Lyonnais -- is most likely to involve a shares for cash exchange that would mean a stock dilution.

Dupont Denant estimated the recapitalisation would mean creation of 79 million new shares. It said the stock could be worth around 250 francs, based on a calculation that it was trading at a 20 to 30 percent discount to 1997 price earnings.
"But the lack of visibility makes us believe great caution should be shown," said Patrick Leclerc of Dupont Denant.

On top of that 15 billion francs, the government may have to find extra funds to soften the terms of a previous rescue package under which Credit Lyonnais made a 123 billion loan to a state-run shell company set up to sell off the bank's assets.
Because of the recent drop in interest rates, Credit Lyonnais has said the shell company repayments do not meet its costs in financing the loan.
The government is believed willing to neutralise the cost of this loan -- implying, newspaper reports suggest, extra state spending of up to 15 billion francs over a number of years.
The government has refused to estimate the cost of the plan, saying it will not be known until it is put into effect.
The cost will reflect the size of capital losses from asset disposals demanded by the Commission in exchange for approving the new state aid.
Rival Societe Generale has already insisted that the Commission take a tough line against any fresh state aid, and has vowed legal action against what it sees as unfair competition.

The shares, floated in the mid-1980s at just under 700 francs, have clawed their way back from a low of 98.60 francs last June. They have been rising steadily amid growing optimism about the bank's outlook but the latest gains were triggered by the article in Les Echos.

"The forecasts for 1997 signal a spectacular rebound -- it should generate this year between 3.4 and 3.7 billion francs of net attributable profit, that is to say, levels comparable to the performances of Banque Nationale de Paris or Societe Generale," the newspaper said.
The bright prospects were due to a strong contribution from market activities, good results from U.S. and Asian operations and a rebound in French retail banking, the newspaper said.
